title: Regularization I - Ridge Regression (L2)
abstract:
The first of the three routes to the bias–variance sweet spot. Ridge regression
reduces overfitting by shrinking the coefficients rather than removing
them: it adds a squared penalty on the coefficients to the loss. This document
derives the closed-form solution, shows why adding $\lambda I$ makes
$X^{\!\top}X$ invertible and therefore fixes multicollinearity, gives the
constraint geometry that explains why Ridge never produces exact zeros, works the
Bayesian interpretation, and covers the practical matters — scaling, not
penalising the intercept, and tuning $\lambda$.

blocks.t: The Idea
From the notes

items: Regularization is used to reduce overfitting.

Ridge regression reduces overfitting by shrinking coefficients,
 not removing them.

Loss $=$ Loss $+$ Penalty — add a squared penalty on
 the coefficients.
Shrinks coefficients but never makes them zero.
Used in cases where all features are important.

blocks.t: The objective

equivalently $\|y-X\beta\|^2+\lambda\|\beta\|_2^2$. Note the sum starts at
$j=1$: the intercept $\beta_0$ is not penalised, because shrinking it
would merely shift every prediction towards zero for no reason.
Why a penalty helps at all

Overfitting has a numerical signature: enormous coefficients that nearly cancel
(Topic 39). A degree-14 polynomial that threads through noise needs coefficients
in the thousands. The penalty makes those coefficients expensive, so the
optimiser will only pay for them if they buy a genuinely large reduction in the
error term. Small coefficients mean a smoother function — and smoothness is
exactly what generalises.

blocks.cap:
The same degree-14 basis under four values of $\lambda$. At
 $\lambda=0$ Ridge is OLS and overfits badly; as $\lambda\to\infty$ every
 coefficient is crushed to zero and the fit becomes a flat line at $\bar y$. The
 useful region is in between.

blocks.t: The Closed Form
Derivation
L(\beta)=(y-X\beta)^{ \top}(y-X\beta)+\lambda\beta^{ \top}\beta
\frac{\partial L}{\partial\beta}=-2X^{ \top}(y-X\beta)+2\lambda\beta=0
\Longrightarrow\quad \left(X^{ \top}X+\lambda I\right)\beta=X^{ \top}y
\boxed{ \hat\beta_{\text{ridge}}=\left(X^{ \top}X+\lambda I\right)^{-1}X^{ \top}y }

Compare with OLS: $\hat\beta=(X^{\!\top}X)^{-1}X^{\!\top}y$. The only
change is $+\lambda I$ — and that one term does all the work.
Why $+\lambda I$ fixes multicollinearity

Recall from Topic 36 that with collinear features $X^{\!\top}X$ is singular or
badly conditioned, so OLS has no unique solution and its coefficients are wildly
unstable. Adding $\lambda I$ shifts every eigenvalue up by $\lambda$:
\text{eig} \left(X^{ \top}X+\lambda I\right)=\lambda_j+\lambda .

Since $X^{\!\top}X$ is positive semi-definite, every $\lambda_j\ge0$, so every
eigenvalue becomes strictly positive for any $\lambda>0$. The matrix is
guaranteed invertible. The condition number falls from
$\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}$ to $(\lambda_{\max}+\lambda)/(\lambda_{\min}+\lambda)$,
which is dramatically smaller when $\lambda_{\min}\approx0$.

This is not a side benefit — Ridge was invented in 1970 by Hoerl and Kennard
precisely to solve the ill-conditioning problem, and the name comes from the
"ridge" of $\lambda$ added along the diagonal.

blocks.cap:
Left: two predictors correlated at 0.99, refitted 200 times. The OLS
 estimate of $\beta_1$ swings wildly around the truth; Ridge's is tightly
 concentrated — slightly biased, far less variable. Right: $\lambda$ is a
 hyperparameter with a clear optimum.

blocks.t: Why Ridge Never Reaches Zero

blocks.cap:
Coefficient paths as $\lambda$ grows. Every coefficient shrinks
 smoothly towards zero, but — as the right panel shows on a log scale — the
 smallest one approaches zero asymptotically and never arrives.

blocks.t: The algebraic reason
In the orthonormal case ($X^{\!\top}X=I$) the Ridge solution is exactly
\hat\beta_j^{\text{ridge}}=\frac{\hat\beta_j^{\text{OLS}}}{1+\lambda} .

Every coefficient is multiplied by the same factor $\frac{1}{1+\lambda}<1$.
Multiplication by a positive number can never produce exactly zero.
It is proportional shrinkage.

Contrast Lasso (Topic 42), whose orthonormal solution is
$\operatorname{sign}(\hat\beta_j)\left(|\hat\beta_j|-\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\right)_{+}$
— a subtraction that clips at zero, which is why Lasso does produce
exact zeros.
The geometric reason

Ridge can be written as a constrained problem: minimise the squared error subject
to $\sum_j\beta_j^2\le t$. The constraint region is a sphere (a circle
in 2-D). The solution is where the elliptical error contours first touch that
sphere.

A sphere has no corners. The tangent point can be anywhere on its surface, and
the set of points lying exactly on an axis has measure zero — so the probability
that a coefficient is exactly zero is zero. The $L_1$ ball, by contrast, is a
diamond whose corners lie on the axes, and contours meet corners very
often. That single difference in shape is the whole of the Ridge/Lasso
distinction.

blocks.cap:
The constrained view. The elliptical contours are the OLS loss; the
 green disc is the $L_2$ constraint. The solution is the tangent point — which,
 because the boundary is round, is almost never on an axis.

blocks.t: The Bayesian Interpretation
Ridge is MAP estimation under a Gaussian prior

Place a prior $\beta_j\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau^2)$ on each coefficient and assume
Gaussian noise $\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$. The posterior is
proportional to likelihood $\times$ prior, and maximising its logarithm gives

So Ridge is exactly the maximum a posteriori estimate with
$\lambda=\sigma^2/\tau^2$. The penalty encodes a belief that coefficients are
probably small — a strong prior ($\tau$ small) means a large $\lambda$.

The parallel result for Lasso uses a Laplace prior, whose sharp peak at zero is
what produces sparsity.
Practical Matters
Scaling is mandatory

The penalty $\sum\beta_j^2$ treats every coefficient identically, but a
coefficient's size depends on its feature's units. A feature measured in rupees
has a tiny coefficient and is barely penalised; the same feature in lakhs has a
coefficient $10^5$ times larger and is crushed. Always standardise before
Ridge — otherwise the regularisation is arbitrary and unit-dependent.

rows: Slight shrinkage; still close to OLS
Bias rises a little, variance falls a lot, total error is minimised
Underfitting — all coefficients crushed, predictions approach $\bar y$
$\hat\beta\to0$; the model predicts the intercept for everything

blocks.t: Naming

Statisticians write $\lambda$; scikit-learn calls it alpha. In
LogisticRegression and SVMs the parameter is $C=1/\lambda$, so
smaller $C$ means stronger regularisation — the inverse
convention, and a common source of confusion (Topic 52).
Code

import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge, RidgeCV, LinearRegression, SGDRegressor
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, GridSearchCV, train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE CLOSED FORM, FROM SCRATCH
# =====================================================================
n, p = 100, 10
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, p))
X[:, 3] = 0.98 * X[:, 0] + rng.normal(0, .1, n)      # near-collinear pair
true_w = np.array([3., -2., 1.5, 2., 0., 0., 0., 0., 0., 0.])
y = X @ true_w + rng.normal(0, 1., n)

def ridge_closed_form(X, y, lam):
    """beta = (X'X + lambda*I)^-1 X'y, with the intercept NOT penalised."""
    Xc, ym = X - X.mean(0), y.mean()               # centre, so no intercept column
    I = np.eye(X.shape[1])
    beta = np.linalg.solve(Xc.T @ Xc + lam * I, Xc.T @ (y - ym))
    return beta, ym - X.mean(0) @ beta

b, b0 = ridge_closed_form(X, y, 1.0)
sk = Ridge(alpha=1.0).fit(X, y)
print("scratch:", b.round(4))
print("sklearn:", sk.coef_.round(4))
print("match:", np.allclose(b, sk.coef_, atol=1e-8))

# lambda = 0 IS ordinary least squares:
print("\nlambda=0 == OLS:",
      np.allclose(ridge_closed_form(X, y, 0.0)[0],
                  LinearRegression().fit(X, y).coef_, atol=1e-6))

# =====================================================================
# 2. WHY +lambda*I FIXES SINGULARITY -- every eigenvalue shifts up
# =====================================================================
G = X.T @ X
ev = np.linalg.eigvalsh(G)
print(f"\nX'X eigenvalues: min {ev.min():.4e}  max {ev.max():.2f}")
print(f"condition number: {ev.max()/ev.min():.3e}")

for lam in [0.0, 0.01, 1.0, 100.0]:
    e = np.linalg.eigvalsh(G + lam * np.eye(p))
    print(f"lambda={lam:7.2f}  min eig {e.min():10.4f}  cond {e.max()/e.min():12.3e}")
# Every eigenvalue rises by exactly lambda, so the matrix is ALWAYS invertible.

# PERFECT collinearity: OLS fails outright, Ridge does not
Xp = X.copy(); Xp[:, 4] = Xp[:, 0]                 # an exact duplicate
try:
    np.linalg.inv(Xp.T @ Xp)
except np.linalg.LinAlgError:
    print("\nOLS: X'X is singular -- no solution")
print("Ridge handles it:", Ridge(alpha=1.0).fit(Xp, y).coef_[:5].round(3))

# =====================================================================
# 3. IT SHRINKS BUT NEVER ZEROES
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'lambda':>10s} {'min |beta|':>12s} {'exact zeros':>13s} {'sum |beta|':>12s}")
for lam in [0.0, 1, 10, 100, 1e4, 1e7, 1e10]:
    c = Ridge(alpha=lam).fit(X, y).coef_
    print(f"{lam:10.0e} {np.abs(c).min():12.3e} {int((c == 0).sum()):13d} "
          f"{np.abs(c).sum():12.4f}")
# The count of exact zeros is ALWAYS 0, even at lambda = 1e10.

# THE ORTHONORMAL CASE: beta_ridge = beta_ols / (1 + lambda)
Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(0, 1, (200, 5)))    # orthonormal columns
yq = Q @ np.array([2., -1., 3., .5, -2.]) + rng.normal(0, .3, 200)
ols_q = LinearRegression(fit_intercept=False).fit(Q, yq).coef_
for lam in [0.5, 2.0, 10.0]:
    rid_q = Ridge(alpha=lam, fit_intercept=False).fit(Q, yq).coef_
    print(f"lambda={lam:5.1f}: ridge == ols/(1+lambda)? "
          f"{np.allclose(rid_q, ols_q/(1+lam), atol=1e-8)}")
# Proportional shrinkage -- multiplication can never produce exactly zero.

# =====================================================================
# 4. THE BIAS-VARIANCE TRADE, MEASURED
# =====================================================================
def bias_var(lam, sims=400):
    ests = []
    for _ in range(sims):
        Xi = rng.normal(0, 1, (60, p)); Xi[:, 3] = .98*Xi[:, 0] + rng.normal(0, .1, 60)
        yi = Xi @ true_w + rng.normal(0, 1., 60)
        mdl = LinearRegression() if lam == 0 else Ridge(alpha=lam)
        ests.append(mdl.fit(Xi, yi).coef_)
    E = np.array(ests)
    bias2 = np.sum((E.mean(0) - true_w) ** 2)
    var   = np.sum(E.var(0))
    return bias2, var, bias2 + var

print(f"\n{'lambda':>8s} {'Bias^2':>10s} {'Variance':>10s} {'Total':>10s}")
for lam in [0, 0.1, 1, 5, 20, 100, 1000]:
    b2, v, t = bias_var(lam)
    print(f"{lam:8.1f} {b2:10.4f} {v:10.4f} {t:10.4f}")
# Bias rises, variance collapses, and the TOTAL has a minimum in between.
# That minimum is why a biased estimator can beat the BLUE one (Topic 40).

# =====================================================================
# 5. SCALING IS MANDATORY
# =====================================================================
Xs = X.copy()
Xs[:, 0] *= 1000                                    # one feature in different units
print(f"\n{'':22s} {'beta_0':>12s} {'beta_1':>12s}")
r_raw = Ridge(alpha=10).fit(Xs, y)
r_scl = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge(alpha=10)).fit(Xs, y)
print(f"{'unscaled':22s} {r_raw.coef_[0]:12.6f} {r_raw.coef_[1]:12.6f}")
print(f"{'scaled':22s} {r_scl[-1].coef_[0]:12.6f} {r_scl[-1].coef_[1]:12.6f}")
# Unscaled, feature 0's coefficient is ~1000x smaller, so the penalty barely
# touches it. The regularisation has become an artefact of your unit choice.

# =====================================================================
# 6. THE INTERCEPT IS NOT PENALISED
# =====================================================================
y_shift = y + 500                                   # shift the target
a = Ridge(alpha=10).fit(X, y).coef_
b_ = Ridge(alpha=10).fit(X, y_shift).coef_
print(f"\ncoefficients unchanged by a target shift: {np.allclose(a, b_)}")
print(f"intercept moved by {Ridge(alpha=10).fit(X, y_shift).intercept_ - Ridge(alpha=10).fit(X, y).intercept_:.1f}")
# If beta_0 were penalised, shifting y would distort every other coefficient.

# =====================================================================
# 7. TUNING lambda
# =====================================================================
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

# RidgeCV uses efficient leave-one-out -- essentially free
rcv = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                    RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(-3, 4, 60))).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"\nRidgeCV chose alpha = {rcv[-1].alpha_:.4f}")
print(f"test R2 = {rcv.score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")
print(f"OLS  R2 = {LinearRegression().fit(X_tr, y_tr).score(X_te, y_te):.4f}")

gs = GridSearchCV(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge()),
                  {"ridge__alpha": np.logspace(-3, 4, 40)},
                  cv=5, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error").fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"GridSearchCV agrees: alpha = {gs.best_params_['ridge__alpha']:.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 8. RIDGE ON A HIGH-DEGREE POLYNOMIAL -- the Topic 39 problem, solved
# =====================================================================
xp = np.sort(rng.uniform(-3, 3, 30))
yp = 0.5*xp**2 - 0.4*xp - 1 + rng.normal(0, .9, 30)

print(f"\n{'model':30s} {'cv MSE':>10s} {'max |beta|':>13s}")
for tag, mdl in [
    ("degree 14, OLS",   make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), PolynomialFeatures(14),
                                       LinearRegression())),
    ("degree 14, Ridge a=0.01", make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), PolynomialFeatures(14),
                                              Ridge(alpha=.01))),
    ("degree 14, Ridge a=1",    make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), PolynomialFeatures(14),
                                              Ridge(alpha=1.))),
    ("degree 2,  OLS (the truth)", make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(2),
                                                 LinearRegression())),
]:
    cv = -cross_val_score(mdl, xp[:, None], yp, cv=5,
                          scoring="neg_mean_squared_error").mean()
    mdl.fit(xp[:, None], yp)
    print(f"{tag:30s} {cv:10.4f} {np.abs(mdl[-1].coef_).max():13.4e}")
# Ridge lets you keep a rich basis and control flexibility with alpha
# instead of having to guess the right degree.

# =====================================================================
# 9. GRADIENT DESCENT VERSION -- for when p is large
# =====================================================================
def ridge_gd(X, y, lam, lr=0.01, epochs=3000):
    Xb = np.c_[np.ones(len(X)), X]
    w = np.zeros(Xb.shape[1])
    mask = np.ones_like(w); mask[0] = 0            # do NOT penalise the intercept
    for _ in range(epochs):
        grad = -(2/len(y)) * Xb.T @ (y - Xb @ w) + 2*lam/len(y) * mask * w
        w -= lr * grad
    return w[0], w[1:]

i_gd, c_gd = ridge_gd(StandardScaler().fit_transform(X), y, lam=1.0)
c_cf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge(alpha=1.0)).fit(X, y)[-1].coef_
print(f"\ngradient descent vs closed form: max diff "
      f"{np.abs(c_gd - c_cf).max():.5f}")

# sklearn's SGD version, for very large p:
sgd = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                    SGDRegressor(penalty="l2", alpha=0.01, max_iter=5000,
                                 tol=1e-6, random_state=0)).fit(X, y)
print("SGDRegressor(penalty='l2') coef:", sgd[-1].coef_[:4].round(3))
Worked Examples
Ridge shrinks the slope as $\lambda$ grows
Centred single-feature case, no intercept, data $x=[1,2,3]$, $y=[2,4,5]$. Ridge objective $\sum (y_i - w x_i)^2 + \lambda w^2$ has closed form
\hat w = \frac{\sum x_i y_i}{\sum x_i^2 + \lambda}
Here $\sum x_i y_i = 2+8+15 = 25$ and $\sum x_i^2 = 14$.

Reading it. Every increase in $\lambda$ pulls $\hat w$ toward zero, but never exactly to zero. The penalty is quadratic, so its pull weakens as $w$ shrinks, and no coefficient is ever removed. That is the defining behaviour of L2.

Practical point. With several features the penalty applies to every coefficient, so features must be standardised first. Otherwise a feature measured in large units gets a tiny coefficient and is penalised less than it should be.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
Regularization is used to reduce overfitting. Three types:
 $L_2$ (Ridge), $L_1$ (Lasso), Elastic Net.

Ridge reduces overfitting by shrinking coefficients, not removing
 them. Loss $=$ Loss $+$ Penalty, with a squared
 penalty:
 $L=\sum(y_i-\hat y_i)^2+\lambda\sum_{j\ge1}\beta_j^2$.

It shrinks coefficients but never makes them zero, so it is
 used when all features are important.

Closed form:
 $\hat\beta=(X^{\!\top}X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^{\!\top}y$. The only change from
 OLS is $+\lambda I$.

That term raises every eigenvalue by $\lambda$, so $X^{\!\top}X+\lambda I$
 is always invertible — which is why Ridge fixes
 multicollinearity and stabilises the coefficients.

In the orthonormal case $\hat\beta^{\text{ridge}}=\hat\beta^{\text{OLS}}/(1+\lambda)$
 — proportional shrinkage, which can never reach exactly zero.

Geometrically the constraint region is a sphere, which has no
 corners, so the tangent point almost never lies on an axis.

Ridge is the MAP estimate under a Gaussian prior, with
 $\lambda=\sigma^2/\tau^2$.

Scaling is mandatory; the intercept is not penalised;
 $\lambda$ (alpha in sklearn) is tuned by cross-validation.
$\lambda=0$ is OLS; $\lambda\to\infty$ crushes every coefficient to zero.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. What does Ridge regression do, in one sentence?

It adds $\lambda\sum\beta_j^2$ to the least-squares loss, shrinking the
coefficients towards zero — accepting a small bias in exchange for a large
reduction in variance.
Q. Why does Ridge never produce exactly zero coefficients?

Two ways to see it. Algebraically, in the orthonormal case it divides each
coefficient by $1+\lambda$, and multiplication by a positive number never yields
zero. Geometrically, the $L_2$ constraint region is a sphere with no corners, so
the tangent point almost never lands on an axis.
Q. How does Ridge fix multicollinearity?

Adding $\lambda I$ raises every eigenvalue of $X^{\!\top}X$ by $\lambda$,
guaranteeing invertibility and collapsing the condition number. The coefficients
become stable and reproducible, at the cost of a small bias.
Q. Ridge is biased. Why prefer it to OLS?

Because Gauss–Markov says OLS is best among unbiased estimators, and total
error is bias$^2$ plus variance. Ridge trades a little bias for a large variance
reduction, so the total can be lower — especially with correlated features or
$p$ close to $n$.
Q. Why must you standardise before Ridge?

Because the penalty $\sum\beta_j^2$ treats all coefficients alike, but a
coefficient's magnitude depends on its feature's units. Without standardisation
the amount of regularisation each feature receives is an arbitrary consequence of
your unit choices.
Q. Why is the intercept excluded from the penalty?

Because shrinking it would pull every prediction towards zero, which is
meaningless — the location of $y$ is not something we want to regularise. It
also makes the fit invariant to shifting the target, which it should be.
Q. How do you choose $\lambda$?

Cross-validation over a log-spaced grid. RidgeCV does efficient
leave-one-out for free by exploiting the closed form. Never pick it by training
error — $\lambda=0$ always wins there.
